pages.title: Carrying the Message: Step 12 in the Big Book (Page 89)
pages.metaDescription: What carrying the message means in Step 12 and Chapter 7 of the Big Book, why working with other alcoholics keeps us sober, and how to actually do it.
pages.h1: Carrying the Message: Step 12 and Working With Others
pages.subtitle: Why the Big Book says helping another alcoholic is the surest way to stay sober ourselves
pages.bodyHtml:
Carrying the message is the heart of Step 12: "Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs" (page 60). The Big Book devotes an entire chapter to it, Chapter 7, Working With Others, and opens with one of the most quoted lines in the whole book: "Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (page 89). Notice what that sentence actually claims. Not that helping others is a nice extra once we feel better, but that it protects our own sobriety more reliably than anything else we can do.

The same page makes it a direct instruction: "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (page 89). Then it tells us why we, of all people, are qualified: "You can help when no one else can" (page 89). Doctors, family, and friends may have tried for years to reach a drinker and failed. But one alcoholic talking honestly to another gets a hearing nobody else gets, because we have been where they are. Our drinking history, the thing we were most ashamed of, becomes the very credential that lets us reach someone still suffering.

Why Working With Others Keeps Us Sober

The Big Book is blunt about our stake in this. Early in the book it says "our very lives, as ex-problem drinkers, depend upon our constant thought of others and how we may help meet their needs" (page 20). That is strong language, and it is meant to be. The alcoholic mind drifts back toward self, and self-centeredness is described on page 62 as the root of our troubles. Twelfth Step work is the practical antidote. When we sit with a newcomer, we cannot stay wrapped up in our own problems. We hear our own story out of someone else's mouth, and we remember exactly what we were saved from.

Chapter 7 also promises something beyond protection. "Life will take on new meaning" (page 89). Watching people recover, watching them turn around and help others, watching a fellowship grow up around us, the book says this is an experience we must not miss. Later in the chapter it goes further still: "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (page 97), and it adds that an occasional kindly act is not enough. This is daily material, not a merit badge we earn once.

How We Actually Carry the Message

The chapter is practical about method. We are told to learn what we can about the prospect first, to approach him when he is ready to listen rather than when he is very drunk, and to talk as one alcoholic to another, sharing our own drinking history before we ever mention a solution (pages 90-91). We describe ourselves as someone who has found an answer, not as someone recruiting for a cause. If he is not interested, we do not force it; the book tells us not to waste time chasing a man who cannot or will not work with us, because our job is to be useful, not to argue anyone into recovery (page 96). And carrying the message is bigger than formal Twelfth Step calls. It is sponsorship, greeting the newcomer at a meeting, sharing honestly, and letting our changed life speak. The book's closing page puts it simply: "Give freely of what you find and join us" (page 164).

The Spiritual Awakening Comes First

Step 12 begins with a condition: having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps. We carry a message we have actually received. That is why the first eleven steps matter so much; without them we have sympathy to offer, but not a solution. The awakening does not need to be dramatic. Appendix II describes most of our spiritual experiences as gradual, of the educational variety (pages 567-568). What matters is that something real has changed in us, and we give it away to keep it. Freely we received, so freely we give. That exchange, one alcoholic helping another, is the engine that has kept this fellowship alive since two men sat down together in Akron in 1935.

faq.q: What does carrying the message mean in Step 12?
faq.a: It means sharing the solution we found through the first eleven steps with alcoholics who still suffer. Step 12 reads in part that having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics (page 60). The message is not just our story; it is the program of recovery that produced our spiritual awakening.

faq.q: What page of the Big Book says working with other alcoholics insures immunity from drinking?
faq.a: Page 89, the opening of Chapter 7, Working With Others. It says practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics, and adds that this kind of work succeeds when other activities fail.

faq.q: Do I have to sponsor someone to work Step 12?
faq.a: No. Sponsorship is one powerful form of Twelfth Step work, but Chapter 7 describes many ways to be useful: making calls on prospects, welcoming newcomers, and simply being available (pages 89-90). Page 97 says helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery, and that can look like any daily act of service to another alcoholic.

faq.q: What if the person I try to help doesn't want to get sober?
faq.a: The Big Book says not to force ourselves on anyone and calls it a waste of time to keep chasing a man who cannot or will not work with us (page 96). We plant the seed, stay friendly if we can, and move on to someone who is ready. The outcome belongs to God; our job is only to carry the message honestly.

pages.title: The 12 Steps of AA: A Big Book Guide (Pages 58-60)
pages.metaDescription: The Twelve Steps as the Big Book presents them on pages 58-60, plus a plain-language guide to each step. Start with Step One and work forward.
pages.h1: The 12 Steps, Big Book Guide
pages.subtitle: The program of recovery exactly as pages 58 to 60 lay it out, one step at a time.
pages.bodyHtml:
Where the Steps Come From

The Twelve Steps are not a list someone wrote for us to admire. They are the path the first members of Alcoholics Anonymous actually took to get sober, written down in Chapter 5 of the Big Book, How It Works. The chapter opens with a promise many of us have heard read aloud at meetings: 'Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path' (page 58). The steps themselves appear on pages 59 and 60, introduced simply as the steps the first members took, 'suggested as a program of recovery' (page 59). Suggested, not commanded. But the book is honest about what half-hearted effort gets us: 'Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point' (page 59).

What the Steps Actually Do

Read in order, the steps tell one story. We admit we are beaten (Step One), come to believe help exists (Step Two), and decide to accept it (Step Three). Then we get honest about our past (Steps Four and Five), let go of what blocks us (Six and Seven), repair the damage we caused (Eight and Nine), and build a daily life of inventory, prayer, and service (Ten, Eleven, and Twelve). Right after listing them, the book boils the whole program down to three ideas on page 60: we could not manage our own lives, probably no human power could relieve our alcoholism, and God could and would if He were sought.

Progress, Not Perfection

Many of us looked at that list and balked. The book saw us coming: many of us exclaimed, 'What an order! I can't go through with it.' (page 60). Its answer is the sentence that has steadied alcoholics for generations: 'We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection' (page 60). No one works these steps flawlessly. We simply stay 'willing to grow along spiritual lines' (page 60), and we start where every one of us started, with Step One. The guides below walk through each step the way the Big Book presents it, page by page, in plain language. Pick a step and begin.

faq.q: What are the 12 Steps of AA?
faq.a: The Twelve Steps are the program of recovery described in the book Alcoholics Anonymous, listed on pages 59 and 60 of the 4th Edition. They move from admitting powerlessness over alcohol in Step One, through a moral inventory and making amends, to prayer, meditation, and carrying the message to other alcoholics in Step Twelve. The book presents them as the steps its first members took, 'suggested as a program of recovery' (page 59).

faq.q: Do you have to work the 12 Steps in order?
faq.a: The Big Book presents the steps as a sequence because each one builds on the honesty and willingness of the one before it. Step Four's inventory follows the decision made in Step Three, and the amends of Step Nine depend on the list made in Step Eight. Most of us work them in order with a sponsor, remembering the book asks only for spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection (page 60).

pages.title: Big Book Fear Inventory — Step 4, Pages 67-68
pages.metaDescription: How the Big Book's fear inventory works: list your fears, ask why you have them, and the remedy on page 68 — trusting God rather than self.
pages.h1: The Big Book Fear Inventory
pages.subtitle: How the Big Book has us review our fears — and what it offers in their place.
pages.bodyHtml:
The Big Book's fear inventory lives on pages 67 and 68, in Chapter 5, How It Works — a few short paragraphs tucked between the resentment inventory and the review of our relationships. Short, but not small. The book introduces fear with unusual force: 'It was an evil and corroding thread; the fabric of our existence was shot through with it' (page 67). If you have ever gotten honest about what actually drove the drinking — and the lying, the hiding, the big talk — you know why the book gives fear its own review.

The Instructions, Step by Step

The directions are plainer than we expect. 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper, even though we had no resentment in connection with them' (page 68). That last clause matters. In the resentment inventory we had already noticed fear sitting underneath entry after entry. Here the book has us list the fears that stand on their own — fear of losing a job, a marriage, our health, our standing, fear of being found out, fear of ending up alone. On paper, each one, by name. Fear does its best work in the dark, and the inventory is simply the act of turning the lights on.

Then comes the question that turns a list into an inventory: 'We asked ourselves why we had them. Wasn't it because self-reliance failed us?' (page 68). We had run our lives on our own strength, our own cleverness, our own plans — and the returns kept shrinking. Self-reliance was the strategy, and fear was the receipt. The book allows that self-reliance was good as far as it went, but it didn't go far enough. When the bet is everything and the bankroll is only ourselves, fear is simply honest arithmetic.

The Remedy the Book Offers

The fear inventory doesn't end with insight; it ends with a change of ground. 'We are now on a different basis; the basis of trusting and relying upon God' (page 68). Instead of demanding that we be big enough for every threat, we hand the outcome to something bigger than us. The practical prayer is right there in the text: 'We ask Him to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be' (page 68). Notice the direction of that prayer — not toward the thing we're afraid of losing, but toward who we might become. And the book's promise for this piece of work is immediate and modest: 'At once, we commence to outgrow fear' (page 68). Commence. It is a beginning renewed daily, not a lightning cure.

Working It Today

If you are on Step Four, take a fresh sheet and write down every fear you can name, whether or not it connects to a resentment. Beside each one, ask the book's question: why do I have it? Where did relying on myself alone actually leave me? Then use the prayer on page 68 for each fear on the list, and bring the whole sheet to your sponsor when you share your Fifth Step. Many of us date the real loosening of fear's grip to that one honest conversation. The Promises even circle back to this work later in the book: 'Fear of people and of economic insecurity will leave us' (page 84). The old fears may still knock. The difference is that we no longer have to answer the door alone.

faq.q: Where is the fear inventory in the Big Book?
faq.a: Pages 67-68 of Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition, in Chapter 5, How It Works. It comes immediately after the resentment inventory instructions and uses the same on-paper approach: 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper' (page 68).

faq.q: How do I do a Big Book fear inventory?
faq.a: List every fear you can name on paper, even the ones with no resentment attached (page 68). For each one, ask the book's own question — why do I have it, and wasn't it because self-reliance failed me? Then pray for the fear to be removed and your attention redirected to what God would have you be (page 68), and review the list with your sponsor in Step Five.

faq.q: What does the Big Book say about fear?
faq.a: It calls fear 'an evil and corroding thread' running through the fabric of our existence (page 67), and treats it as a root problem deserving its own review — not just a symptom of resentment. The remedy it proposes is a change of basis, from relying on ourselves to trusting God (page 68).

faq.q: Does the fear ever actually leave?
faq.a: The book says we 'commence to outgrow fear' at once (page 68) — a beginning that grows with daily practice. Later, among the Ninth Step Promises, it says plainly: 'Fear of people and of economic insecurity will leave us' (page 84).
